name: Amira Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for talking with me, Amira. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in a chilled and frozen food warehouse that supplies about forty supermarkets. I'm in the chiller at five in the morning in a padded jacket and gloves, picking yoghurts, milk and ready meals onto roll cages using a voice headset that tells me the next location. When they brought the headsets in last year, I volunteered to be a super user, which means I'm the one people come to when theirs plays up.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being good at something new before everyone else, and I like the girls on my shift, we pray for each other's families on the group chat. What wears me out is the cold in my fingers by ten o'clock, and the drivers shouting when a cage isn't ready. The freezer section is worse, you can only do twenty minutes before you have to come out.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm married to Daniel, he drives the number 14 bus, and we rent a flat near our church. We've got about five months saved, and we're hoping to start a family in the next two years. I bake celebration cakes at weekends for church people and friends, and I use AI every day, for pricing my cakes, for my budget, and for studying for the team leader test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was overhyped, but the useful bits are still useful. At work I'd keep showing people the shortcuts on the headsets. Online I'd post a picture of my cake with a caption like, the AI didn't bake this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it means the job stays steady and I keep moving up. I'm going for team leader anyway, and the AI tools I already use help me study. Nothing in my plans depended on a revolution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit the team leader assessment in the spring and keep the super user role. I'd grow the cake orders to about four a month, using the AI to work out prices so I don't undercharge. We'd keep putting money aside for when the baby comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Peaceful, really. It's the picture where hard work pays off the normal way. I like that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you undercharge. What did the AI tell you about your cake prices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The AI told me I was charging £40 for a cake that costs me £22 in ingredients and six hours of work. That's less than I earn an hour in the chiller. Now I charge £65 and nobody's complained.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would team leader change things for you and Daniel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About two thousand a year more and no more freezer shifts, which matters when I'm pregnant. Daniel's hours on the bus are long, so a steadier rota for me would help us both. My mum says a family needs one parent with regular hours.

say: I'd say AI was **overhyped**, but the useful bits stay useful.
I'd post my cake online captioned the AI didn't **bake** this.
think: The chiller job stays steady and I keep **moving up** toward team leader.
None of my plans depended on a **revolution**.
do: Sit the **team leader** assessment in the spring.
Grow cake orders to about **four a month** with AI pricing.
Keep saving for when the **baby** comes.
feel: **Peaceful**, because hard work pays off the **normal way**.
S0.quote: The AI told me I was charging £40 for a cake that costs me £22 in ingredients and six hours of work.
fieldNote: She uses **AI daily** for practical ends: pricing, budgeting, studying.
Her **promotion** and family plans don't depend on AI at all.
She already acts as a **super user**, early on new tech.

steps.text: Sit the team leader assessment in the spring
Price celebration cakes with AI and take four orders a month
Keep saving monthly for the baby

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance for anyone willing to learn. At work I'd tell people the headsets were the start, and the ones who learned them didn't get left behind. At church I'd say God helps those who help themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's good for me and hard for some of my friends. The ordering and planning upstairs would change fast, and they'd need people on the floor who understand both the systems and the work. That's exactly where I'm aiming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push for team leader and ask to join any trial of robots or new software. I'd do the free online courses on warehouse systems in the evenings. And I'd keep the cake business going as a second income, because you never put all your eggs in one basket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a little excited. A bit sad for the people who'll struggle, but I can't carry everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Auntie Grace, she's not my real aunt, she's sixty-one. Our oldest picker, Auntie Grace, still writes notes on her glove because the headset confuses her. I'd help her as much as I could, but I'm not sure she'd make it through a big change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you can't carry everyone. Does that sit right with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It sits right with my head, not always with my heart. I believe people should work for what they get, and the company has every right to bring in new things. But I'd still sit with Auntie Grace at break and show her the screens.

say: I'd say it's a **chance** for anyone willing to learn.
At church I'd say **God helps** those who help themselves.
think: It's **good for me** and hard for some friends.
The floor will need people who know **systems and work**.
do: Push for **team leader** and join any new trials.
Take free evening **courses** on warehouse systems.
Keep the **cake business** as a second income.
feel: **Calm** and a little excited, with **sadness** for colleagues who'll struggle.
S1.quote: Our oldest picker, Auntie Grace, still writes notes on her glove because the headset confuses her.
fieldNote: Her traditional **self-reliance** sits alongside real **care** for older colleagues.
She defends the company's **right to automate**.
She aims to be the bridge between **systems and floor**.

steps.text: Volunteer for any robot or software trial in the chiller
Take free evening courses on warehouse management systems
Keep taking weekend cake orders as a second income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening, and anyone who says otherwise isn't thinking about their family. At work I'd say learn what you can, now, while you still have time. At church we'd pray, but we'd also make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it means my picking job is probably gone around 2031, and maybe team leader with it, because the planning part of team leader goes first. And Daniel's bus driving could go when the robots get good, which is the same years. Two jobs in one house both on the same clock, that's what scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any training the company offered on looking after the robots and keep using AI to learn faster than the others. I'd grow the cake business into something bigger, maybe a stall at the Saturday market by next summer. And I'd talk to Daniel about waiting on the baby until we know where we stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, in my chest. I'm a planner, and this is the first picture where my plans might not be enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Daniel the night you heard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Daniel we start saving like the baby is already here, so we're ready either way. He'd say we should trust God, and I'd say God gave us brains as well. Then we'd make a list together at the kitchen table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've always said family comes first. Would you really wait on a baby?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would break my heart, but yes, maybe a year or two. I'd rather bring a child into a house with a plan than into a house full of worry. My mother had me in a hard time and she always said she wished she'd waited.

say: I'd say it's **frightening** for any family.
At church we'd **pray**, but we'd also sit down and make real plans.
think: My picking job is likely **gone around 2031**, maybe team leader too.
Daniel's **bus driving** faces the same clock, so both incomes are at risk.
do: Take any **robot maintenance** training the company offers.
Grow cakes into a **market stall** by next summer.
Talk with Daniel about **delaying the baby**.
feel: **Anxious** in her chest, fearing her **plans** aren't enough.
S2.quote: Two jobs in one house both on the same clock, that's what scares me.
fieldNote: **Both incomes** on the same timeline changes her calm.
She'd consider **delaying a child**, which costs her deeply.
Her faith supports **planning**, not just waiting.

steps.text: Take the company's robot maintenance training when offered
Open a Saturday market stall for cakes by next summer
Delay trying for a baby by a year or two
Save as if the baby is already here

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time if you start now and stop moaning. At work I'd tell people to get on every course going. At church I'd organise a little group to help people learn the computer things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, eight years until robots means I've got time. I'd be team leader by then, maybe moved into the systems side. Daniel's job is the one I'd think about, because he's not as quick with technology as me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for team leader this year and ask to shadow the systems team. I'd help Daniel look at training, maybe as a bus depot controller or something in the office, and use AI to find courses for him. We'd go ahead with the baby next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in charge. It's like a long shift you know will be hard, but you've packed your flask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the church group look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tuesday evenings in the hall, me and a laptop, showing older people how to use the job sites and the AI helpers. Pastor Mark (the pastor at our church) already asked if I'd do something like that. People trust you more when they know your mother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd push Daniel toward an office job, but office jobs go first. Is that right?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You've caught me there. Maybe not the office then, maybe something with people, like training new drivers. I'd have to think harder about that one.

say: I'd say five years is enough if you **start now**.
I'd run a **church group** to teach computer skills.
think: **Eight years** until robots means I have time to move up.
**Daniel's job** on the buses is what I'd really think about.
do: Go for **team leader** and shadow the systems team.
Use AI to find **courses for Daniel**.
Go ahead with the **baby** next year.
feel: **Uneasy** but in charge, like a hard shift with her **flask packed**.
S3.quote: People trust you more when they know your mother.
fieldNote: Her concern shifts from herself to **Daniel's job**.
She'd use her skills to help her **church community**.
She accepts the **contradiction** about office jobs openly.

steps.text: Get the team leader job and shadow the systems team
Use AI to find driver-trainer courses for Daniel
Start trying for a baby next year as planned
Run Tuesday computer classes at the church hall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time to get ready, so there's no excuse. At work I'd keep pushing the courses. At church I'd say plan for your family, don't fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm fine with ten years. I'd be 40 before robots took the warehouse, with children at school and hopefully a cake shop or a systems job. It's the same end, but I'd have time to choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going for team leader and the systems side. I'd have the baby on time, maybe two. I'd save for a small cake shop and maybe open it in five or six years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like the future is something I can build, not something that happens to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the cake shop look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little front room on the high street near the church, with two ovens and a window display. Daniel could do deliveries on his days off. The AI would do my ordering and the robots can wash up, I don't mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that people get comfortable and forget it's coming. Ten years is long enough to get lazy. I'd stick a note on the fridge: 2036.

say: I'd say ten years is enough, so **no excuse**.
At church I'd say **plan** for your family, don't fear.
think: I'd be **40** before robots took the warehouse.
I'd have time to choose a **cake shop** or systems job.
do: Keep going for **team leader** and the systems side.
Have the **baby** on time, maybe two.
Save for a small **cake shop** in five or six years.
feel: **Calm**, the future feels like something she can **build**.
S4.quote: The AI would do my ordering and the robots can wash up, I don't mind.
fieldNote: A decade restores her **calm** and long-range plans.
She sees **AI and robots** as tools for her own business.
Her only worry is **complacency**, hence the fridge note.

steps.text: Keep working toward team leader on the systems side
Have the first baby on time, maybe two children
Save toward a small cake shop near the church

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Daniel and I would both be on the same clock, with a baby on the way or waiting. What would help is the company paying for robot and systems training for everyone on the floor, not just the managers. And small business loans for people like me who want to start something real.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I'd tell my children. I'd tell my children to learn the machines but never stop using their hands. A cake still needs someone who knows when it smells right.

headlineQuote: I'd tell my children to learn the machines but never stop using their hands.
portrait: Amira is a **27-year-old picker** in a chilled food warehouse and the shift's **super user**.
She's married to **Daniel**, a bus driver, and plans a family soon.
She uses **AI daily** and bakes cakes as a side business.
She's calm until AGI comes fast and puts **both incomes** at risk.
Her faith pushes her to **plan**, not just wait.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with both her and Daniel's jobs on the same **clock**.
whatWouldHelp: Company-paid **robot training** for all floor staff.
**Small business loans** for people starting something real.
